title: Why Have We Stopped?
subtitle: Diagnose obstacles and restore useful progress
summary: Pip’s dashboard rewrite stalls despite a busy workshop. Stopping well means checking the desired outcome, diagnosing obstacles, and choosing whether to continue, change direction, or stop. A shared definition of done and honest feedback keep momentum connected to a useful destination.

concepts.title: Stopping rule
concepts.body: Pip asks for more speed; the workshop asks which obstacle to solve. Is a decision missing, a skill unavailable, understanding uneven, or the destination no longer worthwhile? A stopping rule names evidence that the goal is met or needs reconsideration. Pip checks the agreed adoption threshold instead of adding another status meeting. Different reasons for stopping need different interventions—not one louder instruction to move.

steps.text: Pip diagnoses the stoppage before demanding speed.
A stalled project may have several causes.
Compare evidence with the agreed goal and stopping conditions.

concepts.title: Feedback
concepts.body: The progress chart looks calm. A conversation with the people doing the work reveals an unresolved disagreement and a quiet dependency. Feedback compares the actual result with the intended outcome, supplying evidence for the next choice. Pip listens to those accounts alongside support tickets and usage data. Uncomfortable information matters while it can still change the route; a tidy chart is not a reason to ignore it.

steps.text: Pip checks results against the intended outcome.
The chart cannot show every disagreement.
Surface evidence while the route can still change.

concepts.title: Momentum
concepts.body: Tickets close all week, but the regulatory fix remains blocked behind Pip’s dashboard rewrite. Momentum means useful movement toward a goal, not visible busyness. Pip names the next concrete step and its owner, then asks whether the old milestone still serves the destination. If the goal has changed, renegotiating it is execution. More activity cannot make an obsolete objective worth reaching.

steps.text: Pip distinguishes activity from useful movement.
Many completed tasks can coexist with a stalled outcome.
Make the next concrete step and its owner visible.

concepts.title: Finishing
concepts.body: Pip calls the service ready; the operations team asks who supports it. Finishing includes rollout, adoption, cleanup, documentation, communication, and follow-through. The final handoff needs explicit owners and a check that the original problem was addressed. Pip stays attentive through this unglamorous coordination. A technically complete system that nobody can confidently operate has not reached the workshop’s shared finish line.

steps.text: Pip follows the project beyond merged code.
Technical readiness does not establish operating readiness.
Agree support ownership and a post-launch check.

misconceptions.claim: a staff-plus role is mainly about applying a universal formula.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter treats judgment as contextual: identify forces, listen to evidence, and adapt the response to the actual system and people.

misconceptions.claim: A visible activity or artifact proves the work is complete.
misconceptions.correction: Completion requires a useful outcome, shared understanding, and a way to notice whether the decision worked over time.

scenario.title: Decide whether to stop
scenario.context: Pip’s dashboard rewrite misses its adoption goal twice. Some components are useful, but continuing delays a regulatory fix. Should the workshop keep polishing?

options.label: Stop and salvage
options.benefit: Useful components survive while capacity serves the important fix.
options.cost: The workshop must acknowledge sunk effort and rehome partial work.
options.consequence: Pip compares adoption evidence with the goal, preserves reusable pieces, and redirects the team to the regulatory outcome.

options.label: Continue for sunk cost
options.benefit: The team avoids an uncomfortable stopping conversation today.
options.cost: The regulatory fix waits and later cancellation gets more expensive.
options.consequence: The dashboard gains polish while the same adoption gap persists. Pip’s continued activity has not answered the evidence.

scenario.debrief: Past effort cannot choose the next investment. Pip uses outcome evidence to decide what to stop, keep, or redirect.

quiz.question: A project has stopped moving. What helps before demanding more speed?
options: Diagnose the actual obstacle with the people doing the work
Add the same status meeting every day
quiz.explanation: Missing decisions, dependencies, understanding, and changing goals need different responses.

quiz.question: Many tickets close but the desired outcome remains distant. What should the lead inspect?
options: The number of messages in chat
Whether activity still advances the destination
quiz.explanation: Visible busyness can hide a stalled goal or unresolved dependency.

quiz.question: Who should own the operational handoff at the end of a project?
options: Explicit owners agreed before the handoff
quiz.explanation: Finishing includes operational readiness and follow-through, not only implementation.

exercise.prompt: Describe a staff-level decision, the people and terrain involved, and the route by which you will learn whether it worked.
